results.title: H100 vs H200 vs B200: which GPU to rent | GPUBeacon
highlights:
## The one-screen version

- H100 80 GB: default Hopper hour. Rent it when the job fits and you can fill the SMs.
- H200 141 GB: same family, more and faster HBM. Rent it when the KV cache, weights, or optimizer states are the bill.
- B200 180–192 GB: Blackwell. Rent it when FP4 or the new fabric is the reason, and the row is in stock.

Catalog sample on GPUBeacon, on-demand, per GPU: H100 from $1.73, H200 from $3.00, B200 from $3.75. Those are not list prices for every region. They are the cheapest published on-demand hours in the index. Confirm the live SKU. A waitlist B200 at $3.75 is not cheaper than an in-stock H100 at $2.10.

Same GPU count, same hours. H200 only wins if the extra memory drops a card or stops a swap. Do that math on the catalog from-price, then confirm the live row.

...

### H200

H200 is Hopper with a memory upgrade: 141 GB HBM3e and more bandwidth. It is not Blackwell. It will not magically double your tokens per second on a job that already sat inside 80 GB. It will stop you from shrinking context, dropping batch, or adding a second GPU just to hold the KV cache.

### B200

B200 is Blackwell. Catalog rows often say 180 GB; NVIDIA’s SXM story is typically 192 GB HBM3e. Confirm the SKU. FP4 dense around 9 PFLOPS is why the slide exists. Your stack has to speak FP4. Power is part of the product: these nodes sit near a kilowatt. They are not marketplace 4090s with a new badge.

results.title: The GPU Provider Shakeout: What Q1-Q2 Exits Taught | GPUaaS.com
highlights:
H100 spot fell to $1.99 an hour, below the cost basis for debt-financed providers. Five to seven are projected to survive from over a hundred. The mechanism, and what it means for buyers.

...

H100 spot pricing fell to $1.99 an hour during the first half of 2026. That is below the cost basis for providers carrying debt-financed hardware.

Analysis across multiple sources now puts the number of GPU cloud providers likely to survive the next 18 to 24 months as standalone businesses at five to seven. There are well over a hundred competing today.

Key takeaways

- H100 spot fell to $1.99/hr, below the cost basis for debt-financed providers. Five to seven providers are projected to survive the next 18 to 24 months as standalone businesses
- A debt-financed cluster breaks even around 70 to 75% utilization. At 70%, right at the threshold, a 1,024-GPU H100 cluster still loses $80K to $130K a month
- Provider stress is visible before any announcement: capacity rationing, slower response for non-enterprise customers, sudden pricing changes
- Vendor-financed providers must price to cover both debt service and the vendor's revenue cut, so an unexplained premium may be structural rather than opportunistic
- Renewals from 2024-2025 land through late 2026 against a changed standard: sovereignty, geographic resilience, compliance, not just access

...

For buyers, provider financial stress shows up before any announcement does, and the symptoms are specific. Capacity rationing. Lower responsiveness for non-enterprise customers. Sudden pricing changes. Those are what a provider does when utilization is below break-even and cash is tight, and they are visible to a customer well before a shutdown notice.

There is a pricing tell worth understanding too. Providers financed through vendor arrangements carry locked-in cost structures tied to revenue-share terms, so their on-demand pricing has to cover both debt service and the vendor's cut. Providers without vendor-financed capital expenditure can price closer to market because they are not servicing those obligations. A price that seems inexplicably high may be structural rather than opportunistic.

results.title: H100 vs H200 vs B200: what actually changed? · temperature2
highlights:
H200 doubles H100's memory at identical compute; B200 changes architecture entirely, roughly doubling compute too, and its rental price tracks that difference almost exactly.

...

H200 keeps H100's Hopper compute (989 TFLOPS dense BF16, 1,979 dense FP8 per Nvidia's datasheets) but adds HBM3e for 141GB at 4.8 TB/s versus 80GB at 3.35 TB/s. B200 switches to Blackwell silicon, adding native FP4 support and about 2.27x H100's dense FP8 throughput at 180GB and 8 TB/s per GPU.

...

- ▸ H100 and H200 share the same Hopper compute die: 989 TFLOPS dense BF16 and 1,979 TFLOPS dense FP8, per Nvidia's own datasheets. H200 only adds memory: 141GB HBM3e at 4.8 TB/s versus H100's 80GB HBM3 at 3.35 TB/s.
- ▸ B200 is a different architecture, not a Hopper refresh: 4,500 TFLOPS dense FP8 per GPU (2.27x H100), derived from Nvidia's DGX B200 datasheet, plus Hopper's first native FP4 Tensor Core path.
- ▸ NVLink jumped from 4th generation at 900 GB/s per GPU (H100, H200) to 5th generation at 1.8 TB/s on B200, per Nvidia's HGX platform specifications.
- ▸ On 2026-08-26 Ornn Data pricing, H100 rents for $2.68/GPU-hour, H200 for $4.24, and B200 for $6.22. H200's premium buys memory only; B200's buys memory, bandwidth, and compute together.
- ▸ Nvidia doesn't publish a standalone B200 TDP the way it lists H100/H200 at 'up to 700W'; the commonly cited 1,000W figure for the 180GB SXM part comes from an OEM product guide, not an Nvidia datasheet.

...

## The short answer

H100 SXM and H200 SXM share the same Hopper GH100 compute die, so their Tensor Core throughput is identical: 989 TFLOPS dense BF16, 1,979 TFLOPS dense FP8, per Nvidia’s H100 and H200 datasheets. H200’s entire upgrade is memory: 141GB of HBM3e at 4.8 TB/s versus H100’s 80GB of HBM3 at 3.35 TB/s. B200 switches to Blackwell silicon entirely, and per Nvidia’s DGX B200 datasheet an 8-GPU DGX B200 system delivers 36 PFLOPS dense FP8 and 72 PFLOPS dense FP4, which works out to 4,500 TFLOPS dense FP8 and 9,000 TFLOPS dense FP4 per GPU, alongside 180GB of HBM3e at 8 TB/s and 5th-generation NVLink at 1.8 TB/s per GPU, double Hopper’s 900 GB/s. On Ornn Data’s 2026-08-26 pricing, that progression costs $2.68, $4.24, and $6.22 per GPU-hour for H100, H200, and B200 respectively, a curve that tracks compute and memory gains more closely than it tracks hype.

...

| Spec (per GPU) | H100 SXM | H200 SXM | B200 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Memory | 80GB HBM3 | 141GB HBM3e | 180GB HBM3e |
| Memory bandwidth | 3.35 TB/s | 4.8 TB/s | 8 TB/s |
| Dense BF16/FP16 | 989 TFLOPS | 989 TFLOPS | 2,250 TFLOPS |
| Dense FP8 | 1,979 TFLOPS | 1,979 TFLOPS | 4,500 TFLOPS |
| Dense FP4 | not supported | not supported | 9,000 TFLOPS |
| NVLink | 900 GB/s, 4th gen | 900 GB/s, 4th gen | 1.8 TB/s, 5th gen |
| TDP | up to 700W | up to 700W | ~1,000W (OEM figure) |
| Rental price, 2026-08-26 | $2.68/GPU-hr | $4.24/GPU-hr | $6.22/GPU-hr |

The H100 and H200 rows come straight off Nvidia’s own spec tables. The B200 compute and memory rows are derived: Nvidia’s DGX B200 datasheet publishes them at the 8-GPU system level (1,440GB total memory, 64 TB/s aggregate bandwidth, 36 PFLOPS dense FP8, 72 PFLOPS dense FP4), and dividing by eight gives the per-GPU figures above, a method Nvidia’s own HGX platform page independently confirms with matching per-GPU NVLink and Tensor Core numbers for HGX B200. Rental prices are Ornn Data’s compute price index, settled 2026-08-26, and worth reading against compute rather than in isolation: dividing price by dense FP8 throughput puts H100 at about $0.00135 and B200 at about $0.00138 per TFLOPS-hour, nearly the same rate, while H200 costs about $0.00214 per TFLOPS-hour for identical Hopper compute, since its entire premium over H100 buys memory and nothing else. On a memory-per-dollar basis the ranking flips: H200 delivers about 33.3GB per dollar-hour of rental cost, versus 29.9GB for H100 and 28.9GB for B200, meaning H200 is actually the cheapest way to buy raw HBM capacity of the three.

 Der Handelsstart ist für den 5. Oktober 2026 vorgesehen, allerdings ausdrücklich vorbehaltlich behördlicher Zustimmung, wie CME Group in der Ankündigung mitteilte. results.title: How much does it cost to rent an H100 per hour?
highlights:
An H100 SXM rented for $2.68 a GPU-hour on 2026-08-26 on the open market, but the same chip lists for $3.99 to over $7 depending on who sells it.

...

An Nvidia H100 costs roughly $2.68 to $4.29 per GPU-hour on-demand as of late August 2026, with the low end set by blended market rates on Ornn Data's index and the high end by named clouds like Lambda and AWS, and the spread comes from three separable factors: node granularity, commitment length, and provider tier.

...

- ▸ H100 SXM rented for $2.68 per GPU-hour on 2026-08-26 on Ornn Data's blended market index, down 8.5% over 7 days.
- ▸ Lambda Labs' own pricing page lists an 8-GPU H100 SXM node at $3.99 per GPU-hour on-demand, rising to $4.29 for a single GPU.
- ▸ AWS's EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML price a reserved H100 at $5.191 per GPU-hour in US East and US West regions, per a 2026-08-16 survey.
- ▸ The same chip's price varies 3x to 5x across providers because of three separable factors: how many GPUs you rent at once, how far in advance you commit, and whether the seller is a hyperscaler or a bare-metal neocloud.
- ▸ RunPod's SXM pods listed at $3.29 per GPU-hour and Vast.ai's marketplace floor sat as low as $1.87, both as of a 2026-08-16 check.

...

An Nvidia H100 SXM rented for $2.68 per GPU-hour on 2026-08-26 on Ornn Data’s blended compute price index, while the same chip’s own on-demand list price at Lambda Labs sat at $3.99, and a reserved AWS Capacity Block ran $5.191. All three numbers describe the identical piece of silicon. The one skill this post hands you: read an H100 quote and know which of three separable factors, node granularity, commitment length, or provider tier, explains why it isn’t the number you saw on a different site last week.

## The short answer

There is no single H100 price, only a spread that runs roughly $1.87 to $7 per GPU-hour depending on who you ask and what you’re buying. Ornn Data’s blended index put H100 SXM at $2.68 per GPU-hour on 2026-08-26, down 8.5% over the trailing week. Lambda Labs’ own pricing page lists an 8-GPU SXM node at $3.99 per GPU-hour on-demand, rising to $4.29 for a lone GPU, while AWS prices a prepaid EC2 Capacity Block at $5.191 per GPU-hour in US East and US West as of a 2026-08-16 survey. RunPod’s SXM pods listed at $3.29 the same day, and Vast.ai’s peer-to-peer marketplace floor dropped as low as $1.87. None of these figures is wrong; they’re pricing different products (spot marketplace capacity, on-demand branded cloud, prepaid reserved capacity) that happen to run on the same chip.

...

An H100’s rental price is set by three mostly independent levers, and a quoted number usually only tells you where it sits on one of them. The first is node granularity: an H100 SXM GPU is normally sold as part of an 8-GPU server connected by NVLink, and a provider renting out fewer than all eight is still on the hook for whatever’s left over. Lambda Labs’ pricing page shows this directly: $3.99 per GPU-hour for the full 8-GPU node, climbing to $4.09 for 4 GPUs, $4.19 for 2, and $4.29 for a single GPU, a premium for buying in a smaller unit than the hardware’s native shape.

The second lever is commitment length. On-demand pricing, where you start an instance and pay by the hour with no advance notice, sits at the top of the range because the provider bears the risk that capacity goes unsold. Reserved products invert that: AWS’s EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML let a buyer lock in a P5 instance for a fixed future window, and because the provider now has certainty instead of risk, the price comes down, to $5.191 per GPU-hour in US East, US East (Ohio), and US West (Oregon), and $4.720 elsewhere, per a 2026-08-16 pricing survey. Spot and interruptible instances go further in the same direction: the renter accepts the risk of losing the instance on short notice, and the provider passes the savings through.

The third lever is provider tier, and it’s the one that explains most of the headline spread. A hyperscaler like AWS sells H100 capacity bundled with its networking, storage, security, and support stack, all priced into the hourly rate. A bare-metal neocloud like Lambda Labs or RunPod sells closer to the raw chip with less surrounding infrastructure, which is part of why their on-demand H100 rates land below AWS’s. A peer-to-peer marketplace like Vast.ai goes a step further, reselling spare capacity from many independent hosts of varying reliability, which is how its floor gets down to $1.87 while carrying none of a hyperscaler’s guarantees.

...

| Source | Product | Price | Date |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ornn Data | Blended market index, H100 SXM | $2.68 / GPU-hour | 2026-08-26 |
| Lambda Labs | On-demand, 8x H100 SXM node | $3.99 / GPU-hour | live pricing page |
| Lambda Labs | On-demand, 1x H100 SXM | $4.29 / GPU-hour | live pricing page |
| Lambda Labs | On-demand, 1x H100 PCIe | $3.29 / GPU-hour | live pricing page |
| RunPod | On-demand pod, H100 SXM | $3.29 / GPU-hour | surveyed 2026-08-16 |
| Vast.ai | Marketplace floor | as low as $1.87 / GPU-hour | surveyed 2026-08-16 |
| AWS | EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML, US East/West | $5.191 / GPU-hour | surveyed 2026-08-16 |
| AWS | EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML, other regions | $4.720 / GPU-hour | surveyed 2026-08-16 |

...

The RunPod, Vast.ai, and AWS Capacity Block figures come from a survey published by IntuitionLabs on 2026-08-16, which explicitly separates AWS’s prepaid Capacity Blocks from its standalone on-demand EC2 rate, a distinction worth keeping straight since the two aren’t the same purchase. Across the full set IntuitionLabs surveyed, on-demand H100 rates spanned $1.49 (a promotional low) to $6.98 per GPU-hour, a roughly 4.7x range for what is, at the silicon level, the same Nvidia H100 die.

...

Comparing prices across these sources only works if you’re comparing the same product, and it’s easy not to notice you aren’t. AWS’s $5.191 Capacity Block figure and a neocloud’s $3.99 on-demand figure look like the neocloud is cheaper, but Capacity Blocks are prepaid and reserved while the neocloud number is pay-as-you-go with no commitment; the honest comparison is Capacity Blocks against AWS’s own on-demand P5 rate, or against another provider’s reserved product, not across purchase types. Regional pricing adds a second trap: AWS’s own Capacity Block survey shows a $0.471 per GPU-hour gap between US East/West and other regions for the identical instance type, so a quote from one region says nothing reliable about another.

...

H100 pricing has been sliding as Blackwell-generation GPUs pull the highest-paying training workloads onto newer hardware, leaving more H100 supply competing for inference and mid-size training jobs, which is consistent with Ornn Data’s 8.5% weekly and 1.5% monthly declines measured on 2026-08-26. For the specifics of what changed between generations, see H100 vs H200 vs B200: what actually changed?. Watch the index at /gpu/h100-sxm/ for whether the decline continues as more neocloud capacity comes online, and watch whether AWS narrows the gap between its Capacity Block and on-demand P5 rates as Hopper-class demand cools relative to Blackwell. A sustained move of the blended index below $2 per GPU-hour would mark H100 crossing from premium training silicon into commodity inference capacity, the same transition A100 made after Hopper launched.
